vignette:
Arun has spent fifty of his fifty-eight years on the water. The sea had been his language, the rhythm of the tides his internal clock. He knew its moods, from the placid turquoise of a summer morning to the churning grey of a monsoon squall. His boat, the *Meera’s Grace*, named for his late wife, was more a part of him than his own left hand. He could read the sky and smell a coming storm hours before the weather service issued a warning. But seven months ago, the sky gave no warning.

It was a clear afternoon, the sun warm on his neck. The nets were full. Then, the world tilted. A rogue wave, monstrous and indifferent, rose from a calm sea. It was a wall of dark water that seemed to blot out the sun. Arun remembers the shriek of the wind that came with it, a sound he’d never heard before, and the splintering crack of the outrigger. He was thrown against the console, the impact stealing his breath. For a long, silent moment, suspended in chaos, he was sure he was meeting Meera. He saw her face, not as she was at the end, but as she was on their wedding day. Then the cold shock of the water erased everything. He was tangled in the nets, the weight of his catch pulling him down into the blackness. He fought, his lungs burning, his limbs heavy and useless, until his hand miraculously found the frayed end of a rope.

He was found hours later by another fishing boat, clinging to a piece of the wreckage, hypothermic and disoriented. His village celebrated his survival as a miracle. Arun felt no miracle. The man who came back to shore was a stranger to himself.

Now, Arun wakes up at 4 a.m., just as he always has. But instead of heading to the docks, he sits in the dark of his small kitchen, nursing a cup of tea he doesn’t taste. His son, Rohan, has taken over the boat repairs and the fishing runs. Arun offers excuses—his shoulder, his back, the damp air making his joints ache. The truth is, he cannot bring himself to look at the water. Some days, the sight of the gentle waves lapping the shore makes his heart hammer against his ribs so hard he feels sick. The smell of salt and diesel, once the smell of his livelihood, now brings the taste of panic to the back of his throat.

He spends his days in a state of restless vigilance. A car backfiring on the road sends a jolt through his entire body. He finds himself scanning the horizon from his porch, not for weather patterns, but for an unnamed, unseen threat. He feels a constant, low-grade hum of anxiety, a tightness in his chest that never fully unwinds. Sleep offers no escape. He’s lucky if he gets two hours before the nightmare comes: the wall of water, the crushing weight, the feeling of his lungs filling with the sea. He wakes up gasping, tangled in his sheets, the phantom cold clinging to his skin.

Rohan tries to talk to him, as does his daughter-in-law. They bring him his grandson, a bright-eyed boy whose laughter used to be Arun’s greatest joy. Now, the sound is muffled, as if he’s hearing it from underwater. He feels a profound and hollow distance from them, a chasm of experience he cannot bridge. He feels shame—a fisherman afraid of the sea is no fisherman at all. He sees the worry in his son’s eyes and it curdles into a bitter anger he can’t explain, so he says nothing, retreating further into a silence as vast and empty as the ocean now seems to him. He is a ghost in his own home, haunted not by the memory of his wife, but by the memory of the man who died at sea, even though his body somehow washed back to shore.
